items.q: ezgmail.unread() is called on an account with three unread conversations. What does it return?
options: A list of GmailMessage objects, one for each unread email
A list of GmailThread objects, one for each unread conversation
A list of strings that hold the subject lines
rationales: It asks the Gmail API for threads (users/me/threads with the query label:UNREAD), so the objects are threads; a thread fetches its messages with one more request when messages is first read.
The subject is an attribute of a message that a thread holds; the function returns the thread objects, not text.

items.q: An EmailMessage is built with set_content(text), add_alternative(html, subtype='html') and add_attachment(data, ...). What is the content type of the whole message?
options: multipart/alternative
text/html
multipart/mixed
rationales: multipart/alternative is the inner part that holds the text and the HTML; with an attachment added, the message becomes a multipart/mixed that holds it.
text/html is the type of one inner part, not of the message.

items.q: What does email.utils.parseaddr('real@example.com, evil@example.net') return in Python 3.13 and 3.14?
options: ('', 'real@example.com')
It raises ValueError
rationales: That is the answer only with strict=False; the default is strict, so a string that holds two addresses is not an address.
parseaddr does not raise; it returns empty strings for input it cannot take as one address.

items.q: A program sends a message whose To header says jon@example.org, but passes ['jon@example.org', 'hidden@example.org'] as the recipients. Who receives it?
options: Both addresses, and the hidden one appears nowhere in the text
Only jon@example.org, because the header lists only him
Neither, because the server refuses a header that does not match
rationales: The server delivers to the recipients of the envelope (RCPT TO), not to the header; the header is only text.
The server never compares the two; on the local server the message was accepted with the From header being whatever the sender wrote.

items.q: A plain text of 161 characters from the basic GSM set is sent as an SMS. How many messages does it use?
rationales: One message holds 160 characters of 7 bits (140 bytes), so the 161st character needs another.
A character is not a message; a message carries 140 bytes.

items.q: A 100-character text has one dotless i (ı) in it. Compared with the same text without it, how many messages does it need?
options: The same number; one character does not matter
More: the whole text is sent as UCS-2, which holds 70 characters a message
Fewer: Unicode is a more compact encoding
rationales: One character outside the GSM sets changes the encoding of the whole text.
UCS-2 uses 16 bits a character, twice the 7 bits of GSM-7 in a message of 140 bytes, so fewer characters fit.

items.q: AT&T's support article says its email-to-text service was shut down on June 17, 2025. What does that show about an address such as 5555550100@txt.att.net?
options: It still works, because the address is correct
A gateway that worked once can stop working, and the chapter's table still lists it
Only the MMS address stopped working
rationales: A correct address is not enough when the provider has ended the service.
The notice names the email-to-text and text-to-email service, so both the SMS and MMS domains are affected.

items.q: A poll answer holds two JSON objects, one on each line. What does json.loads(text) do with the whole text?
options: It returns a list of the two objects
It raises JSONDecodeError (Extra data)
It returns only the first object
rationales: JSON has no format that holds two objects after one another; a list needs brackets and commas.
It does not stop after the first object; it checks that nothing follows it.

items.q: A message to ntfy has 2049 characters, each a dotless i (ı), and the limit is 4,096 bytes. Is it within the limit?
options: Yes, 2049 is less than 4096
No, it is 4098 bytes in UTF-8
Yes, ntfy counts characters
rationales: The limit counts bytes, and the dotless i takes two bytes in UTF-8.
The limit is in bytes.

items.q: The chapter's topic is the name 'AlSweigart' and 8 random characters (ZPgxBQ42). Why is secrets.token_urlsafe(16) a better topic?
options: It is shorter, so it is easier to type
It gives 128 bits, where 8 characters of 62 give 47.6 bits, and the topic is the only secret
It is encrypted by ntfy
rationales: It is longer (22 characters), and being easy to type is the opposite of secret.
ntfy does not encrypt the topic; it is part of the URL and shows in logs, and without access control the topic name is the password.

items.q: The command-by-mail program checks a password in the message body and not the From address. Why?
options: A From header is whatever the sender wrote, so it proves nothing
The From address is encrypted
Gmail removes the From address from incoming messages
rationales: The header is plain text.
Gmail keeps the header, and the sender can write any address there.
